RSUs vs. Stock Options

Startups pay part of your compensation in equity, and the offer letter rarely explains it. This lesson covers the two most common forms — stock options and restricted stock units — what each is worth, when each is taxed, and what to do at the three decision points that actually arrive: leaving the company, exercising early, and choosing between offers.

Before anything else — commit to an answer

Your offer letter from Halyard, a startup, says: “Equity: 10,000 shares.” Halyard’s common shares are currently valued at $6.00 each. Is your equity worth $60,000?

After this lesson, you can:

✓Compute what a grant of options or RSUs is worth today and at a future share price, including the cases where the answer is $0.
✓Name the taxable moment, the income type, and the amount for RSUs, nonqualified options, and incentive stock options.
✓Say what happens to each kind of grant when you leave a company, and decide whether to exercise vested options, with real numbers.
✓Explain what early exercise plus an 83(b) election changes, its 30-day deadline, and the risk it takes on.
✓Compare two equity offers and justify a choice by value, tax treatment, and downside.
Next · §1 Why startups pay in equity ↓
§1 · Why startups pay in equity

Equity stands in for salary a startup cannot pay

A large company can offer a high salary because it has profits. A startup is usually spending investor money and has none. So it offers something it does have: a share of what the company might become. If the company grows, that share can be worth far more than the salary you gave up. If it fails, the share is worth nothing. That trade is the reason your offer letter has an equity line.

Employee equity comes in two main contracts. A stock option is the right to buy shares at a fixed price. An RSU — a restricted stock unit — is a promise that the company will hand you shares. Which contract you hold decides what you pay, when you owe tax, and what happens when you quit. The two employees below hold one each, at the same company, and we follow both through the lesson.

Stock options

Ana — 10,000 options, $2.00 strike

Ana joined Halyard two years ago. Her grant lets her buy up to 10,000 common shares at $2.00 each. It vests over 4 years with a 1-year cliff.

RSUs

Ben — 2,500 RSUs

Ben joined the same day. His grant promises him 2,500 common shares as they vest — same 4-year schedule, same cliff, no purchase price.

Halyard’s numbers, used in every example below: common shares are currently valued at $6.00 each (the company’s 409A appraisal — §7 explains that term), and investors most recently paid $9.00 for preferred shares.

Next · §2 What each one is ↓
§2 · What each one is

One is a right to buy; the other is a promise of shares

Commit first

Halyard hits trouble and the share value falls from $6.00 to $1.50. Whose grant is worth more now — Ana’s 10,000 options at a $2.00 strike, or Ben’s 2,500 RSUs?

Stock option

A right to buy at a fixed price

Ana may buy shares at the strike price set on her grant date — $2.00 — no matter what the shares are worth later. Buying is called exercising, and it costs real money. The option’s value is the gap between the share value and the strike, called the spread. If the share value sits below the strike, exercising would mean paying more than the shares are worth, so the option’s value floors at zero. It never goes negative, because a right is not an obligation.

10,000 options · $2.00 strike
share value $6.00
($6.00 − $2.00) × 10,000 = $40,000
RSU

A promise of the shares themselves

Ben buys nothing. When a unit vests and the company delivers it, he owns a share outright. No strike price, no exercise decision, no cash out of pocket — a delivered RSU is worth exactly what the share is worth, at any price above zero. The “restricted” part: until delivery, a unit is only a contractual promise. Ben holds no share, no vote, and no dividend right unless his plan says otherwise.

2,500 RSUs · no strike
share value $6.00
$6.00 × 2,500 = $15,000

The strike price

26 USC §422 ↗ Fixed on grant day. It is why an option can be worth $0 — and why it costs money to use.
Where the number comes from

Startups set the strike at the share’s appraised fair market value on the grant date. For incentive stock options the tax code requires it:

…the option price is not less than the fair market value of the stock at the time such option is granted… 26 U.S.C. § 422(b)(4) (incentive stock options) — Cornell LII

Nonqualified options are priced the same way in practice, because a below-market strike triggers penalties under a separate rule, § 409A. The practical result: your strike is the company’s share value on the day you were granted — so options only become valuable as the company grows after you join.

Vested is not exercised

Vesting makes options yours to use. Exercising — paying the strike — turns them into shares. A vested option is still just a right: Ana can hold it unexercised, spend nothing, and lose nothing but the right itself if it expires. This distinction matters in §5, because vested options usually expire about 90 days after you leave a job, while exercised shares stay yours.

Both grants, priced at every share price

More shares with a strike, or fewer shares free and clear — which grant wins depends entirely on where the share price ends up. The lines cross at $2.67: below it Ben’s grant is worth more, above it Ana’s is.

§3 · Vesting

Vesting: both grants arrive on a schedule

Commit first

Ana’s grant vests over 4 years with a 1-year cliff. Suppose she had quit after 10 months. How many of her 10,000 options would have vested?

Neither grant is yours on day one. Both vest on a schedule, and the standard startup schedule is 4 years with a 1-year cliff: nothing at all vests during your first year; at the 1-year mark the whole first year vests at once (25% of the grant); after that, the rest vests in equal monthly pieces until year four.

The cliff exists so a hire who does not work out leaves with nothing. The monthly schedule after it exists so that every extra month you stay earns a fixed slice — 1/48th of the grant.

Vesting means different things for the two instruments, and the difference matters later. For Ana, a vested option is a right she may use — she still has to pay to exercise it. For Ben, a vested RSU normally becomes a delivered share — except at private companies like Halyard, where plans usually add a second condition before delivery. §4 explains why.

The standard schedule

After the cliff, each month adds 1/48th of the grant. At month 36, for example, 36/48ths — 75% — has vested.

§4 · How each is taxed

Each instrument has its own taxable moment

It is natural to assume equity is taxed when you sell it. For employee equity that assumption is usually wrong, and the mistakes are expensive. Each instrument has one moment when ordinary income tax lands, and that moment is different for RSUs, nonqualified options, and incentive stock options.

Commit first

Halyard goes public. Both of Ben’s delivery conditions are met, and 2,500 shares land in his brokerage account at $8.00 each. He sells nothing — he wants to hold long term. Does he owe tax this year?

RSU taxes — ordinary income at delivery

26 USC §83 ↗ The day shares are delivered, their full market value is wages — whether or not you sell.
The rule

Delivered shares are “property transferred in connection with the performance of services,” and the tax code’s timing rule for such property is:

…the excess of— (1) the fair market value of such property … at the first time the rights … are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture … over (2) the amount (if any) paid for such property, shall be included in the gross income of the person who performed such services… 26 U.S.C. § 83(a) (abridged) — Cornell LII
Read § 83(a) in full
If, in connection with the performance of services, property is transferred to any person other than the person for whom such services are performed, the excess of— (1) the fair market value of such property (determined without regard to any restriction other than a restriction which by its terms will never lapse) at the first time the rights of the person having the beneficial interest in such property are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, whichever occurs earlier, over (2) the amount (if any) paid for such property, shall be included in the gross income of the person who performed such services in the first taxable year in which the rights of the person having the beneficial interest in such property are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, whichever is applicable. The preceding sentence shall not apply if such person sells or otherwise disposes of such property in an arm’s length transaction before his rights in such property become transferable or not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture. 26 U.S.C. § 83(a) — Cornell LII

Since Ben paid nothing for the shares, “the excess over the amount paid” is simply their full value. It is taxed as wages — ordinary income, on his W-2 — the year of delivery.

Ben’s delivery, priced
2,500 units delivered · share value $8.00
wages on W-2: $8.00 × 2,500 = $20,000
withholding: the broker usually sells a slice of the shares to cover it (“sell-to-cover”)
any later gain above $8.00: capital gain when he sells

Nonqualified option (NSO) taxes — ordinary income at exercise

IRS Topic 427 ↗ Exercising is the taxable moment: the spread is wages, even though you received no cash.
The rule

Ana’s options are nonqualified (NSOs) — the default kind. For options like hers, with no readily determinable market value at grant, the IRS puts it this way:

…there’s no taxable event when the option is granted but you must include in income the fair market value of the stock received on exercise, less the amount paid, when you exercise the option. IRS Topic No. 427, nonstatutory options without a readily determinable fair market value — irs.gov

Note what is not taxable: the grant, and vesting. The tax waits for the moment Ana chooses to exercise — then lands on the spread, as W-2 wages with withholding due, even though she spent cash rather than receiving any.

Ana exercises 5,000, priced
exercise 5,000 · strike $2.00 · share value $6.00
cash she pays Halyard: $2.00 × 5,000 = $10,000
ordinary income: ($6.00 − $2.00) × 5,000 = $20,000
any later gain above $6.00: capital gain when she sells

Incentive stock option (ISO) taxes — deferred, with two catches

26 USC §422 ↗ No regular tax at exercise — but AMT can apply, and the favorable treatment has holding-period conditions.
The rule

Some startup option grants are incentive stock options — a tax-favored category. For statutory options, the IRS says:

…you generally don’t include any amount in your gross income when you receive or exercise the option. However, you may be subject to alternative minimum tax in the year you exercise an ISO. IRS Topic No. 427, statutory stock options — irs.gov (two sentences joined; order as in source)

The favorable ending — the whole gain over the strike taxed as long-term capital gain — requires holding the shares long enough:

…no disposition of such share is made by him within 2 years from the date of the granting of the option nor within 1 year after the transfer of such share to him… 26 U.S.C. § 422(a)(1) — Cornell LII

Sell before both periods run and the sale is “disqualifying”: the spread is generally taxed as ordinary income after all. And the AMT catch is real — exercising ISOs with a large spread can trigger alternative minimum tax in the exercise year even though regular tax is zero. This lesson flags AMT rather than teaching its arithmetic; before a large ISO exercise, run the numbers with a tax professional.

The same exercise, as ISOs
exercise 5,000 ISOs · strike $2.00 · share value $6.00
regular ordinary income now: $0
AMT income adjustment: $20,000 — may trigger AMT this year
hold 2 yrs from grant and 1 yr from exercise, then sell: gain over $2.00 is long-term capital gain
sell sooner: the spread generally becomes ordinary income (a “disqualifying disposition”)

Why RSUs exist at all

If options tax later and cost employees nothing until they choose to exercise, why did big private companies switch to RSUs? The answer is a chain of cause and effect, and you can predict its middle step yourself.

From options to double-trigger RSUs

1 · The starting point

At a young startup, options work well. The strike is set at a low share value, the potential upside is large, and nothing is taxed at grant or vesting. Employees pay nothing unless they choose to buy.

2 · The incentive that builds up

The company succeeds and stays private for years. The share value climbs to many times the early strikes — so a new hire’s strike is now high. Their options gain less per share, can end up underwater, and exercising means paying cash plus tax on the spread for shares that still cannot be sold.

3 · The response — you predicted it

Late-stage companies stopped granting new hires options and started promising shares outright, delivered as they vest: an RSU program. No strike to pay, no underwater risk — a share is worth something at any price.

4 · The problem that fix created

Delivered shares are taxed under § 83(a) at their full value — as we just saw. At a company that is still private, that means employees owing real tax on shares they cannot sell.

5 · The fix for the fix

The double trigger. Private-company RSUs now typically require two things before delivery: time vesting and a liquidity event — an IPO or acquisition. Delivery, and therefore tax, waits until the shares can actually be sold. That is why Ben’s §4 shares arrived at the IPO, not at his vesting dates.

Predict step 3

It is 2007. You run compensation at a successful late-stage private company. Share value is up 20× and options have stopped attracting senior hires — the strikes are too high. What do you offer instead?

§5 · Leaving the company

Leaving: vested options come with a deadline

Commit first

Ana quits Halyard today with 5,000 vested options. The new job is hectic, so she does nothing about them for six months. What has happened to the 5,000?

Options at departure

Unvested: canceled. Vested: a countdown starts.

Unvested options are canceled the day employment ends. Vested options survive — but only briefly. The standard plan gives a post-termination exercise window of about 90 days: exercise within it (pay the strike, owe tax per §4) or the options expire worthless. Some companies extend the window to years; that is worth checking before you resign, not after.

For ISOs, the deadline is not just the plan’s — it is in the statute. ISO tax treatment requires that you exercised while employed or within 3 months of leaving:

…at all times during the period beginning on the date of the granting of the option and ending on the day 3 months before the date of such exercise, such individual was an employee… 26 U.S.C. § 422(a)(2) (abridged) — Cornell LII
RSUs at departure

Delivered: yours. The rest: usually gone.

Shares already delivered are simply yours — leaving changes nothing about them. Unvested units are forfeited, like unvested options.

The awkward middle case is double-trigger RSUs that are time-vested but undelivered because no IPO or acquisition has happened yet. Plans genuinely differ: many keep those units alive until an expiration date (often seven years from grant), so a later IPO still delivers them; some cancel them at departure. There is no standard answer — this one you read your own plan for.

Notice what Ben never faces: no exercise window, no cash decision, no deadline. The leaving problem is mostly an options problem.

Decision desk: Ana’s 90 days

Ana’s options are NSOs. Exercising all 5,000 vested options inside the window means paying the strike and the withholding on the spread — for private shares she cannot sell:

Strike cost — $2.00 × 5,000$10,000
Ordinary income — ($6.00 − $2.00) × 5,000$20,000
Withholding due on that income (32% assumed)$6,400
Cash Ana must find today$16,400
Paper value of the 5,000 shares$30,000
What the shares are worth if Halyard fails$0

Your call — there is no designated right answer here. Pick what you would do, and see what each choice trades away.

§6 · Early exercise and the 83(b) election

Early exercise: paying tax at today’s price instead of tomorrow’s

Commit first

Halyard allows early exercise. Priya exercises all her options on her first day: strike $2.00, share value $2.00, spread $0. She files no paperwork with the IRS. Two years later her shares vest, when the share value is $10.00. What happens at vesting?

Some plans let you exercise options before they vest — “early exercise.” You pay the strike now, and the company keeps the right to buy unvested shares back at cost if you leave. Why would anyone pay early? Because of where § 83 puts the taxable moment.

Priya’s problem above: early-exercised shares are still “subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture” until they vest, so § 83(a) waits — and then taxes each batch of shares as it vests, at its value that day. Her $0-spread purchase turned into $8.00 per share of ordinary income, measured at prices she never chose. The election in § 83(b) exists to flip that measurement date:

The 83(b) election

26 USC §83(b) ↗ Choose to be taxed now, at today’s value — then vesting is a non-event and later growth is capital gain.
The rule
Any person who performs services in connection with which property is transferred to any person may elect to include in his gross income for the taxable year in which such property is transferred, the excess of— (A) the fair market value of such property at the time of transfer … over (B) the amount (if any) paid for such property. 26 U.S.C. § 83(b)(1) (abridged) — Cornell LII
An election under paragraph (1) … shall be made not later than 30 days after the date of such transfer. Such election may not be revoked except with the consent of the Secretary. 26 U.S.C. § 83(b)(2) (abridged) — Cornell LII
Read § 83(b)(1) in full
Any person who performs services in connection with which property is transferred to any person may elect to include in his gross income for the taxable year in which such property is transferred, the excess of— (A) the fair market value of such property at the time of transfer (determined without regard to any restriction other than a restriction which by its terms will never lapse), over (B) the amount (if any) paid for such property. If such election is made, subsection (a) shall not apply with respect to the transfer of such property, and if such property is subsequently forfeited, no deduction shall be allowed in respect of such forfeiture. 26 U.S.C. § 83(b)(1) — Cornell LII
Priya’s two timelines
No election — § 83(a) appliesday 1: buy at $2.00, spread $0, no tax
each vest date: ordinary income on (value that day − $2.00)
at $10.00: $8.00/share as wages
sale: capital gain only above the vest-date values
Timely 83(b) — measured on day 1day 1: ordinary income on spread = $0.00
vest dates: nothing happens for tax
sale: everything above $2.00 is capital gain
(long-term once held over a year)

Two risks come with the election. First, cash at risk: Priya paid $2.00 × every share on day one, for stock that may become worthless — or be repurchased at cost if she leaves before vesting. Second, a cost written into the statute itself: if the shares are forfeited, “no deduction shall be allowed in respect of such forfeiture” — tax paid on an election is not refunded. And the 30-day deadline has no extensions: miss it and § 83(a) applies for good.

§7 · Reading an offer

Reading an offer: five questions in order

Commit first

A recruiter tells you: “Investors just paid $9.00 a share, so your 10,000 options at a $2.00 strike are worth $70,000.” What is wrong with that math?

Two share prices exist at every startup

Investors’ preferred price and the common-share appraisal are different numbers for different shares.
Preferred — $9.00 at Halyardwhat investors paid in the last round
comes with extra rights: paid back first
if the company sells low (a “liquidation
preference”), and others
Common (409A) — $6.00 at Halyardwhat employees’ shares are appraised at
by an independent “409A valuation”
sets your strike price at grant
the honest basis for paper-value math

Employee grants are common shares. Recruiters quote the preferred price because it is bigger. When you price a grant, use the 409A common value — and remember both numbers are estimates until there is a real sale.

You now have every piece the checklist needs. When an offer arrives — or when you want to understand the grant you already hold — ask five questions, in this order. Each answer determines what the next one means.

Checklist hidden while you rebuild it from memory below — it comes back when the rebuild is complete.

  1. Which instrument? Options or RSUs — and if options, NSO or ISO. Nothing else in the offer can be interpreted until this is known.
  2. What fraction of the company? Shares granted ÷ fully diluted shares outstanding. 10,000 shares means nothing by itself; ask for the denominator.
  3. What are the prices? The strike (if options), the current 409A common value, and the last preferred price. Now you can compute paper value — on the 409A number.
  4. What is the schedule — and the exits? Vesting and cliff, the post-termination exercise window, and for private-company RSUs, the delivery triggers and what happens to time-vested units if you leave.
  5. Where are the tax moments? Using §4: when will ordinary income land, on what amount, and can you cover it? For options, is early exercise offered, and is an 83(b) election worth it?

The checklist, worked on an offer

the offer on the desk:
“12,000 options, $3.00 strike, standard vesting.
fully diluted: 40,000,000 shares.
last round: $8.00 preferred. current 409A: $5.00.”

What this lesson does not cover

  • This is not tax or legal advice. It teaches the federal rules’ shape so you can ask better questions. Before exercising a large grant or filing an 83(b), talk to a tax professional.
  • State taxes. Everything here is US federal. States add their own income tax, and moving between states mid-vest complicates RSU income sourcing.
  • AMT arithmetic. §4 flags when AMT can apply to ISO exercises; computing it (Form 6251) is out of scope.
  • Your plan’s actual terms. Exercise windows, early-exercise availability, double-trigger details, and what happens to time-vested undelivered RSUs all vary by plan document. The checklist tells you what to look for; the plan is the authority.
  • Dilution and preferences in depth. Future funding rounds shrink your fraction, and liquidation preferences can make common shares worth far less than preferred in a low sale. This lesson introduces the two-price gap; modeling exit waterfalls is its own topic.
  • Other instruments. ESPPs, restricted stock awards, phantom equity, and profits interests exist and are not covered.

The transfer task: apply the five questions to a real grant document.

Open your actual grant agreement or a real offer letter (or a friend’s, or a public sample) and run the five questions of §7 against it in writing. Two are usually not answerable from the document alone — the fully diluted share count and the current 409A value. Draft the email asking for them; companies answer it more often than people expect.

Sources: 26 U.S.C. §§ 83, 422 (Cornell LII) · IRS Topic No. 427 · IRS Publication 525. Quotations verbatim, with abridgments marked. Fictional company; all prices invented for teaching. Built 2026-07-20.

Quick Reference

Stock option

Right to buy at the strike price fixed at grant. Value = (share value − strike) × shares, floored at $0. Vested ≠ exercised: exercising costs cash and is the taxable moment (NSO).

RSU

Promise of shares, no purchase. Worth share value × units once delivered. Private-company plans usually deliver only after time vesting AND a liquidity event (double trigger).

Vesting

Standard: 4 years, 1-year cliff (25% at month 12), then 1/48th monthly. Nothing before the cliff.

NSO tax

No tax at grant or vesting. At exercise: spread = ordinary income (W-2, withholding due). Later growth: capital gain at sale. (Topic 427.)

ISO tax

No regular tax at exercise, but the spread is an AMT adjustment. Long-term capital gain on the whole gain requires no sale within 2 years of grant and 1 year of exercise, and exercise while employed or within 3 months of leaving (§422). Otherwise taxed like an NSO.

RSU tax

At delivery: full share value = ordinary income (§83(a)), regardless of selling. Later growth: capital gain.

83(b) election

For early-exercised (unvested) shares: elect within 30 days of purchase to be taxed on the spread now instead of at each vest. Zero spread → zero income now; later growth becomes capital gain. Irrevocable in practice; no deduction if shares are forfeited.

Leaving

Unvested equity: gone. Vested options: typically 90 days to exercise or lose (ISO statute: 3 months). Delivered RSU shares: yours. Time-vested undelivered RSUs: plan-dependent.

Two prices

Preferred = investors’ price, with extra rights. Common (409A) = employees’ appraised value; sets strikes and honest paper-value math.

Full sources 26 U.S.C. § 83 — Cornell LII 26 U.S.C. § 422 — Cornell LII IRS Topic No. 427 — Stock options IRS Publication 525 — Taxable and Nontaxable Income
